| **Fix** | `fetchTickerFlowAndGamma` now routes the real `recent` rows through `tapeWindowCoverage` (the SAME evidence `get_helix_tape_analytics` reports) and passes the ANALYSED span into `compareSidesFrom`. The flow side emits `window_hours` = actual span (evidence), `window_hours_requested` = the 168h intent (provenance), and `window_limit_reached` = the tell that the count bound before the window did. New pure `flowWindowPhrase(actualHours, actualMinutes, limitReached)` builds the one-liner: it names the measured span (in minutes when sub-hour, so a 40-min burst is never printed as "0h"), appends "print-capped" when the limit bound, and — critically — when NO print carried a usable time it says nothing (or "most recent prints"), never falling back to the requested window. Tool-def updated to tell the model `window_hours` is the analysed span and to read `window_limit_reached` before quoting it as a lookback. |
| **What was deliberately NOT changed** | The 500-print `limit` and 168h request are unchanged — they are the correct population selection (recent-ordered, session-sized, shared with `get_helix_tape_analytics` per #2528); the fix DISCLOSES the coverage, it does not widen the fetch. The card's `as_of_utc` beside the ET `as_of` is kept (a deliberate machine-orderable instant, not a bare-UTC defect). `window_hours` stays unrounded in the numeric field (roundFloats owns the model boundary); only the display STRING rounds, to 1dp with a minutes fallback. |
| **Regression guard** | 4 tests in `helix-thermal-compare.test.ts`: the card carries the analysed span, the requested intent, and the limit tell as three separate fields and the sentence says "54m, print-capped" not "168h"; `flowWindowPhrase` names a sub-hour span in minutes (never rounds a ~2min span to 0h); uses hours rounded to 1dp for multi-hour spans; and returns no measured window (never the request) when no print carried a time. Existing fixture tests (`window_hours` echoed, summary names the window) still pass unchanged. |
| **Gates on Node 20.20.2** | `npx tsc --noEmit` clean · `helix-thermal-compare.test.ts` 28/28. |
| **Status** | FIXED — this PR. Not yet live-verified (held by the pure-helper tests; the `window_hours`/`window_limit_reached` fields must be re-read against a live RTH tape where the 500-print limit binds inside the session). |

## 2026-08-21 — [FINDING, P2 Meridian] The earnings report printed raw HTML entities — "Will S&amp;P 500", "Wall Street&#39;s" — while Largo showed the same headline clean — FIXED

> **kind:** `FINDING`

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Symptom** | Measured on prod during RTH, the BEKE earnings report rendered **`Stock Market: Will S&amp;P 500 Open Up or Down Today?`** as its analyst-cluster headline and **`…Forecast Changes From Wall Street&#39;s Most Accurate Analysts`** in CATALYST BRIEFS — entity and all, on a member's screen. |
| **Scope, measured at the API** | `/api/market/meridian/event?id=earnings:BEKE:2026-08-21` served **9 strings carrying raw entities across 6 fields**: `catalysts[].title`, `earnings_headlines[].title` (×3), `analyst_revisions[].title` (×2), `price_targets[].summary`, `catalyst_briefs[].title`. Two entity forms in play — named (`&amp;`) and numeric (`&#39;`). Every Benzinga-sourced free-text field on the desk was affected; this is not one bad headline. |
| **Root cause — the repo already had the fix** | `sanitizeFeedText` / `decodeHtmlEntities` in `src/lib/largo/sanitize-feed-text.ts` has decoded exactly these since the LARGO-6 hardening work. Meridian's enrichment shapers never called it: `shapeHeadlines` did `String(r.title).trim()`, `shapeAnalyst` did `String(r.title ?? "").trim()`, and the catalyst-brief and price-target shapers passed the provider string straight through. So **the same Benzinga headline read clean through Largo and raw through the desk** — one product, two answers. |
| **Not merely cosmetic** | `shapeAnalyst` derives the **firm** from the title (`/^([^:]+):/`) and the **action** from keyword tests; `loadPriceTargetRows` parses a **price target number** out of title+teaser+body. Parsing encoded text puts entities inside a derived `firm` value the desk displays, and lets a numeric entity hide a character the parser is looking for. The fix decodes **before** those parses, and two tests pin that ordering by source position — reversing it is the easy regression. |
| **A second defect the test found** | `sanitizeFeedText` does `String(s ?? "")`, so a feed row whose `title` arrived as an object yields the literal text **`[object Object]`** — a string a panel would render as a headline. Found by the totality test, not by reading the code. `meridianFeedText` drops non-strings instead. The same hole exists on the Largo side of `sanitizeFeedText`; **flagged, not edited from this lane.** |
| **Fix** | New pure `src/lib/meridian/meridian-feed-text.ts` — `meridianFeedText` (decode + de-markup, non-strings dropped) and `meridianFeedTextOrNull` (absence stays absence: an empty headline is `null`, not an empty string to render). It **delegates** to `sanitizeFeedText` rather than copying its entity table, because two tables drift and then the same headline reads differently on two surfaces — which is this bug, in reverse. Wired into all four shaping sites. |
| **Blast radius** | `meridian-earnings-enrich.ts` (`shapeHeadlines`) and `meridian-catalyst-enrich.ts` (`shapeAnalyst`, `loadPriceTargetRows`, `shapeCatalystBriefs`). Display/normalization only — no number, gate, score, ranking or verdict changes. `channel` keeps its old precedence (`channel` then `type` then null) with the same empty-string-is-absent behaviour. |
| **Regression guard** | `src/lib/meridian/meridian-feed-text.test.ts` (+13), driven by the **exact strings copied from the live response**: `&amp;` and `&#39;` decode; genuine smart quotes around ‘Neutral’ survive undamaged; no live string still holds an entity; nullish/non-string inputs never produce `[object Object]`; `&nbsp;`-only is absent, not blank; markup cannot survive; **`&amp;amp;` decodes exactly one level** (over-decoding is its own defect); all four shapers are wired; the decode precedes both the firm parse and the price-target parse; and Meridian carries no second entity table. |
| **Non-vacuity** | Five mutants, all caught: non-strings stringified again (1 fail); `shapeAnalyst` back to a raw trim (3); headlines back to a raw trim (2); the price-target summary un-decoded (1); Meridian growing its own local decoder (3). Restored: 13/13 pass. |
| **Gates on Node 20.20.2** | `npx tsc --noEmit` clean · `npm test` **9491 pass / 0 fail / 1 skipped** · `npm run build` clean · `npx eslint` clean on all four changed files. |
| **Status** | FIXED — this PR. Not yet live-verified; the proof owed is a re-read of the same event id showing 0 entity-bearing strings where 9 were measured. |

## 2026-08-21 — [FINDING, P2 Meridian] The Signal Orbit diagram was 61px wider than its panel and three labels painted inside the neighbouring panel — FIXED

> **kind:** `FINDING`

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Symptom** | On the Report tab at 1440×1000, the orbit label **`Fundamentals` ran straight into the Earnings Track Record's `25-11-10` with no gap at all**, reading as one string. `HELIX flow` and `YoY trajectory` also crossed the panel border. Found by `meridian-interaction-audit` as `"Fundamentals" ∩ "25-11-10" 2x12px`, reproduced in two runs 15 minutes apart at different spot prices (17.67 → 17.73), so not transient. |
| **The audit under-reported it** | 2×12px is the intersection of two TEXT-NODE boxes, and only that one date happened to sit at that y. The structural fact is much larger, and a screenshot showed it immediately: the label had left its panel entirely and crossed **both** panel borders. |
| **Measured on prod, every number a `getBoundingClientRect`** | `.ms-orbital` 755.52 → 1131.52 (**376px**) · `.mr-panel` 741.72 → 1070.27 (328.55px, 12.8px padding, **content ≈ 302.9px**) · next `.mr-panel` starts 1079.86. Overflow **61.25px**. `Fundamentals` +32.62px past its panel and **23.03px inside the next one**; `HELIX flow` +25.12 / 15.53 inside; `YoY trajectory` +14.00 / 4.41 inside. |
| **Root cause** | `MIN_ORBITAL_SIZE` is **376** — the diagram refuses to draw smaller because below that its own rim labels collide, and `.ms-orbital` sets its box from that geometry rather than from the caller's prop. The report panel asks for **310**, gets 376, and sits in a grid whose track floor was a flat `20rem` (320px) leaving ~303px of content. **The track floor was never told what the diagram needs.** The raising of the floor to 376 carried the note *"the component already sizes its box from `geo.size` … so raising the floor is enough — no call site has to know"*; the grid was the call site that did need to know. Note the panel was already ~7px too narrow for the **requested** 310, so this was latent before the floor moved. |
| **Fix** | `.mr-grid-orbital` sets its track floor to `calc(var(--mr-orbital-box) + 1.6rem + 2px)` — the box plus `.mr-panel`'s own horizontal padding and border. `--mr-orbital-box` is written by `MeridianEarningsReportPanel` from **`orbitalGeometry(...).size`**, the shipping geometry, not from the `size` prop — passing the prop would reserve 310px for a box that draws at 376, which is the same defect one layer up. |
| **Verified in a real engine before shipping** | A local Chromium laid out the actual stylesheet rules at the measured grid width of 1004.8px: `.mr-grid-orbital` → **2 tracks of 497.6px**, panel content **470.4px**, the 376px diagram ending **107.82px inside** the panel's right edge. The untouched `.mr-grid` in the same page → `328.531px` ×3, which **reproduces the live measurement of 328.53 exactly** — so the model is not inventing its own layout. |
| **The trade-off, stated plainly** | The Report analytics grid goes from three columns to two at 1440px. That is the cost, and it is the right one: better one column fewer than text from one panel printed on top of another. Dealer Structure and the track-record bars both gain ~50% width. Only the grid that CONTAINS an orbital is affected — `.mr-grid` is unchanged, so Estimates and History keep their density. |
| **Not fixed here, deliberately** | The four ellipsised orbit labels (`Vector expected move`, `Street / analysts`, `News & catalysts`, `Insider activity`) are the deliberate `labelMaxW` cap, which derives from the 376px box and is unchanged by this. They carry full `title` + `aria-label` and expand on hover. |
| **Regression guard** | `src/lib/meridian/meridian-orbital-panel-fit.test.ts` (+6): the floor is derived from `--mr-orbital-box` and is not a literal; the reserved chrome is read from `.mr-panel`'s **actual** padding and border, so changing the panel's padding fails the test; the component feeds `orbitalGeometry(...).size` rather than the prop; both orbital states (310→376 clamped, 400 unclamped) are covered; the old track really was too small by >70px; and the base `.mr-grid` is untouched. |
| **Non-vacuity** | Five mutants, all caught: a hard-coded `25.5rem` floor instead of the derived one (2 fail); reserving one side of padding instead of two (1); passing the requested size instead of the clamped one (1); dropping the grid class (1); widening every panel grid rather than only the one with an orbital (1). Restored: 6/6 pass. |
| **Gates on Node 20.20.2** | `npx tsc --noEmit` clean · `npm test` **9484 pass / 0 fail / 1 skipped** · `npm run build` clean · `npx eslint` clean. |
| **Status** | FIXED — this PR. Live proof owed: re-measure the same page and confirm **0** labels past `.mr-panel`'s right edge, where three were measured. |

## 2026-08-21 — [FINDING, P1 Largo/Meridian] Meridian was not reachable from Largo at all, and the system prompt documented three routes that are all DENIED — FIXED

> **kind:** `FINDING`

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Why this exists** | Post-close Largo-mastery pass: *"your product must be completely understandable and queryable through Largo."* It was not. |
| **Finding 1 — no tool** | **0 of 127** Largo tool descriptions mentioned Meridian, and `runLargoTool` had no Meridian case. The desk's entire event surface — timeline, earnings intel, OpEx pin accuracy, macro release history, FDA priors — was unreachable. |
| **Finding 2 — the documented path is refused** | `product-knowledge.ts` told the model, in the system prompt, to reach Meridian three ways: `call_internal_api: GET /api/market/meridian/timeline`, `/event`, `/lookup`. **All three are denied by the read allowlist** — `isReadAllowed(p,"GET")` is `false` for each, so every one returns `denied_not_read_allowlisted`. `/api/market/earnings-calendar` **is** allowlisted, which is what makes the contrast measurable rather than theoretical. Documented guidance pointing at a path that cannot work is worse than no guidance: the model tries, fails, and improvises. |
| **Finding 3 — the only real path is a keyword-gated PUSH** | `meridianTimelineForLargo` is injected by `largo-terminal.ts` only when `questionWantsMeridianPrefetch()` fires. Measured over 24 realistic member questions: **8 pass, 33%**. The misses are the natural phrasings — *"What are the big catalysts this week?"*, *"When does NVDA report?"*, *"Is there an FOMC meeting this week?"*, *"When is the next OpEx?"* — while the passes need internal jargon (*"catalyst calendar"*, *"earnings intel"*, *"macro desk"*, *"opex preview"*). `post about $TSLA` passes and `post about $PLTR` misses, because eight tickers are hardcoded in the regex. Even when it fires: 7 fields per item, capped at 12 items over 7 days, truncated to 4000 chars, into a block labelled for social content. |
| **Finding 4 — Meridian was not a registered product** | `LargoProduct` listed SPX_SLAYER, HELIX, THERMAL, VECTOR, NIGHT_HAWK, TRACK_RECORD, MARKET, CATALYSTS, PLATFORM. Meridian was the only desk missing — a product with no registry identity cannot be planned for. |
| **Fix** | Two tools: **`get_meridian_timeline`** (the ranked ET calendar; filters `kind` / `impact` / `ticker` / `days_ahead` / `limit`) and **`get_meridian_event`** (one event's full detail). Both registered in `capability-registry.ts` under a new `MERIDIAN` product, and `product-knowledge.ts` now names the tools and states plainly that the three `call_internal_api` routes are denied. |
| **Shaping is not optional** | The raw timeline measured **151,595 chars (~38k tokens)** live, of which `earnings_analytics_rows` alone is **111,348 (73%)** — a desk grid, not an answer. The tool drops it and **says so, with the row count**, because a reader cannot tell a dropped field from an empty one. Result: *"what are the big catalysts this week"* returns **4,240 chars — a 97% reduction**. |
| **Performance — the cache key was the whole problem** | `loadMeridianTimelineResponse` enriches every earnings name with an options chain; a cold 14-day call did not finish in 500s. The HTTP route and `cron/meridian-warm` share `meridian:timeline:v1:<ET-today>:<days>` and the cron warms **21**. Because the key includes the day count, a tool fetching the caller's 7 would **miss the warm entry every time**. The tool now always fetches 21 and narrows in the pure layer: measured **15.4s cold, 4ms warm**. |
| **A bug this tool found in its own first live call** | `expected_move_pct` came back **0** for NVDA, whose implied move is 5.33%. Root cause was mine: `Number(null)` is `0` and `Number.isFinite(0)` is `true`, so the coercion published **absence as a measured zero** — on **83 of 90** earnings items, every one of which is genuinely `null` upstream. Fixed with an explicit `v == null \|\| v === ""` guard. The unit tests missed it because the fixture *omitted* the field, and `Number(undefined)` is `NaN` — absent-as-undefined and absent-as-null took different paths. Re-verified live: **zero=0**, 150 null / 4 positive across 154 items. |
| **Refusals explain themselves** | A malformed id returns the fix, not just a failure — `"garbage" is not a Meridian event kind…`, `A macro event needs its full id… the event name is part of the key and cannot be guessed`. Measured 2–52ms, with no network call. `bad_event_id` / `event_lookup_failed` / `not_found` are distinct, because only the last one means the event is absent. |
| **Two registry guards caught real mistakes** | The repo's own `registry.test.ts` rejected the first draft twice, correctly: a missing capability entry, and `get_meridian_event` classified `as_of` when it accepts a `date` and can therefore reach a past print. It is now `point_in_time` — the class that can answer *"how did this name trade its last four prints"*, which is most of the reason the tool is worth having. |
| **Regression guard** | 11 tests in `meridian-timeline-for-largo.test.ts` (window narrowing vs fetch width, `impact` meaning that-bar-or-above, sort order, truncation reported, null-normalization, argument clamping, and the absence-vs-zero case) and 6 in `meridian-event-id.test.ts` — including a **drift guard that runs this resolver and Meridian's own `parseMeridianEventId` over the same ids** and fails if they disagree, and a guard pinning the three denied routes so nobody re-adds the old guidance without opening the gate. Non-vacuous: removing the absence guard fails test 4; removing the id mirror fails the drift guard. |
| **Still open, deliberately not fixed here** | Only **4 of 154** earnings items on the live timeline carry an `expected_move_pct` at all (2.6%), while `get_earnings_history` has NVDA's 5.33% readily. That is a coverage gap in the timeline's implied-move overlay, not a defect in these tools — raised separately rather than widened into this PR. |
| **Gates on Node 20.20.2** | `npx tsc --noEmit` clean · `npm test` **9089 pass / 0 fail** · `npm run build` clean · `npx eslint` clean. |
| **Shared files** | `run-tool.ts` (two new cases), `tool-defs.ts` (two new defs), `system-prompt.ts` (one line), `product-knowledge.ts` (the Meridian section), `capability-registry.ts` (one union member, two entries). All additive; no existing tool's behaviour changed. |
| **Status** | FIXED — PR #2545 (draft). Not yet live-verified in production. |

## 2026-08-21 — [FINDING, P1 Largo/Night Hawk] Largo cited a 40% Night Hawk win rate over 5 plays; the real window was 74 resolved at 50% — FIXED

> **kind:** `FINDING`

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Symptom** | Asked "over the last 30 days, how many Night Hawk plays resolved, how many are pending, and what is the win rate?", live Largo answered: **"5 plays. 2 resolved. 3 remain open. Win rate: 40% (2 wins / 5 total)."** Ground truth from `/api/market/nighthawk/analytics?window=30` minutes earlier: **74 resolved, `win_rate` 0.5**. Every figure a member would quote as the product's credibility was wrong. |
| **How it was found** | Not by reading code. I could not size `get_nighthawk_outcomes` from this sandbox (no DB reach, and no HTTP surface exposes its raw rows), so I tested it **end-to-end through the live product** — which is better evidence than a byte count, because it measures what the member actually receives. |
| **Root cause — the measured half** | The tool shipped `fetchNighthawkOutcomeAnalytics`'s **raw rows and no computed rate**, while its own description says *"use to cite credibility (e.g. hit-rate over 30d)"*. So the model derived the rate itself and got both the numerator and the **denominator** wrong — "2 wins / 5 total" where the decided set was 2. This repo already carries the rule it broke: `get_spx_vs_nighthawk_comparison` exists expressly so *"the model never subtracts two other tools' numbers itself"*. |
| **Root cause — the truncation half, CONFIRMED** | Asked to report the tool's own `analytics.rows.length`, Largo said **5** at `window_days=30` (true 74) and **78** at 90 (true 108). Two plausible wrong numbers is the signature of reading a partial payload. **Since confirmed directly**: asked whether its raw tool result ended with the transport's literal `…[truncated]` marker, the model answered **TRUNCATED** and named `analytics` as the last top-level key it could see — so the cut lands inside `analytics`, and neither `pending_count` nor the sibling `pending` list ever arrived. The same probe answers **COMPLETE** for the already-fixed `get_zerodte_record` (last key `plays`), so it discriminates rather than always saying truncated. |
| **Both mechanisms closed by one change** | Both are closed by the same change: the aggregate is now computed **server-side** (no arithmetic left to the model) **and** the row list is bounded and lean (nothing left to truncate). |
| **Fix** | `nighthawkOutcomesForLargo` returns the **same `getNighthawkMetrics(windowDays)`** that backs `/api/market/nighthawk/record`, so the number Largo cites and the number the member's own record page shows cannot drift apart. That metric is already rule-7 correct — `win_rate` is **null, never a fabricated 0**, `decided_count` is the denominator the rate must be printed with, and `low_n` marks a sample too small to read as a record. Aggregates first; a bounded lean sample (≤40 rows, `fitRowsToBudget`) last; blob columns dropped; `plays_note` says outright to quote `win_rate`/`decided_count` and **never count the rows**. |
| **Blast radius** | `run-tool.ts`'s `get_nighthawk_outcomes` case only (my lane's tool); the `pending` list from `fetchPendingNighthawkOutcomes(7)` is preserved. `/api/market/nighthawk/record` and `/api/admin/nighthawk/analytics` are untouched — this makes the tool agree with them rather than changing them. Third instance of the truncation class in this lane after `get_zerodte_record` and `get_nighthawk_edition`; the two earlier fixes' shared helper is what this reuses. |
| **Regression guard** | `src/lib/largo/product-reads.test.ts` (+5): the result carries `total_resolved`/`pending_count`/`win_rate`/`decided_count`/`low_n` (the aggregates the model would otherwise derive); it fits `MAX_TOOL_RESULT_CHARS`; a sampled row list states its true total and tells the reader not to count rows; the blob columns are absent; and a DB-less call degrades to an explicit unknown rather than reporting 0 resolved. |
| **Not a trading-behaviour change** | No gate, rail, sizing, exit rule or grading function is touched — the grading is unchanged, only its *reporting*. No `sim:0dte` before/after is owed. |
| **Gates** | `npx tsc --noEmit` clean · `npm test` **8857 pass / 0 fail** (Node 20.20.2) · `npm run build` clean · `npx eslint` clean. |
| **Status** | FIXED — PR #2480. |

## 2026-08-21 — [FINDING, P1 Largo/core] Largo declines dealer-positioning questions post-close although the cached matrix is warm — the tool is never called — REPRODUCED (fix is Largo-core, flagged for coordinator)

> **kind:** `FINDING`

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Symptom** | ~13:17–13:25 ET (17–25 min after the cash close), `POST /api/market/largo/query` answers every dealer-positioning question with **"I couldn't pull enough live data to answer that — try naming a ticker or asking about SPX structure"**, on 3/3 retries, using only the `live_feed_capture` / `platform_vitals_prefetch` prefetch steps and **never calling `get_positioning`**. It is not thermal-specific: a Night Hawk question returned "internal error … desk tools did not complete cleanly", and "What is SPX structure?" — the decline message's OWN suggestion — also declined. |
| **Proof the data was there** | At the same minute, `GET /api/market/gex-positioning?ticker=SPY` returned `available:true, spot 766.27, gamma_posture "short", net_gex, net_vex +$332B, vanna_posture "positive"`, fresh `asof` — and `?ticker=QQQ` returned `call_wall 735`. The matrix cache is warm; `get_positioning` (which reads it) answers directly. So the decline is **false absence**: the data is one tool call away and Largo does not make it. |
| **Why it matters** | Members use Largo overnight, pre-market, and on weekends — most of the clock. In that window Largo is currently unable to answer questions its own tools can answer, and worse, the decline message advises the user to "ask about SPX structure", which then also declines (the exact self-contradiction `empty-answer-fallback.test.ts` was written to prevent, recurring through a different path). A Night Hawk turn returns a bare "internal error", which is a harder failure than a decline. |
| **Scope / root cause (not yet pinned)** | CROSS-CUTTING, not the thermal surface. The thermal tools + data are healthy (verified: `get_positioning`, `get_gex_heatmap`, `/heatmap` all serve full data post-close). The failure is upstream in the Largo QUERY PIPELINE — the model returns an empty answer (→ `empty-answer-fallback.ts`) without exercising its tool loop, or a prefetch step (`live_feed_capture`) errors/returns thin and short-circuits the turn. Likely `src/lib/largo/core/*` (plan/prefetch) + `largo-live-feed.ts`, not `get_thermal_compare`/`helix-thermal-compare`. |
| **Reproduction** | `scripts/audit/largo-availability-probe.mjs` (added here) pairs each question with an independent `get_positioning` availability check and flags `DECLINED_WITH_DATA` — a decline while the answering tool reports the data present. Pure verdict logic in `lib/availability-verdict.mjs` (5 unit tests). Live run 2026-08-21 13:25 ET: **3/3 DECLINED_WITH_DATA**, exit 1. `INDETERMINATE` is returned when the data is not independently confirmed, so honest absence is never graded as a defect. |
| **Deliberately NOT fixed here** | The fix is in the Largo core query pipeline (out of the thermal-surface lane) and has broad blast radius across every desk. This PR adds the reproduction harness and this record so the owning lane can route it; it changes no product code. **Flagged for the coordinator.** |
| **Gates** | Node 20.20.2 · `availability-verdict.test.mjs` 5/5 · `node --check` + eslint clean on all three files · live probe reproduces (exit 1). |
| **Status** | OPEN — reproduced + harnessed; product fix belongs to Largo-core and is flagged for the coordinator, not attempted in this thermal-lane PR. |

## 2026-08-21 — [FINDING, P2 Helix] The signal follow-through rate carried a read-time as_of but no DATA-time scope — a rate with no window — FIXED

> **kind:** `FINDING`

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Symptom** | `get_helix_signal_outcomes` served `summary.continuation_rate_pct` (e.g. "62.5% over 40 graded") stamped with `as_of` = the READ time. It disclosed the COUNT scope (`rows_summarized`) but no TIME scope: nothing said WHEN those graded fires occurred. Measured live during RTH on 2026-08-21 at 09:43 ET, the follow-through ledger's most-recent graded rows were **entirely from the prior session** — 12 fires spanning 30 minutes of 2026-08-20 (19:30–20:00 UTC = 15:30–16:00 ET) — yet the payload stamped `as_of` = today 09:43 ET beside the rate. A model (or the desk) reading it would present a half-hour of yesterday's afternoon as today's live signal performance. |
| **Why this is structural, not incidental** | The ledger holds the 50 most-recent rows, and a signal cannot be graded until forward bars exist (the 1h checkpoint), so early in EVERY session the graded population is necessarily a prior session's — the read-time `as_of` and the data-time diverge maximally exactly when a member is most likely to ask "how are the signals doing today?" The only per-row time the model saw was on the newest 20 shown rows (`fired_at`/`fired_session`); the summarized population is up to 50, so the OLDEST bound of the rate was invisible and the span was not derivable from the payload. |
| **Root cause** | `summarizeHelixSignalOutcomes` computed counts and a rate but no fired_at span, and `helixSignalOutcomesForLargo` projected the scalars + `as_of` (read time) with no data-time bound. Same class as the compare-card window (#2567: claimed window vs actual coverage) and the C1 session-anchor work — a number published without the time or scope that gives it meaning. |
| **Evidence** | Ran the REAL `summarizeHelixSignalOutcomes` over the REAL live `/api/market/helix/signal-outcomes` rows (pre-deploy, production data shape): aggregate `graded_window` = `{oldest_session: 2026-08-20, newest_session: 2026-08-20, span_hours: 0.50}`, `newest graded session == today (2026-08-21)? false`. Both signal types (split_flow 7g, velocity_spike 5g) resolved to the 2026-08-20 window. Earlier the same morning the graded set was 40 fires over 2026-08-20 14:00–16:30 ET — the population rolls, the "all prior-session" property holds. |
| **Blast radius** | `get_helix_signal_outcomes` (Largo) — aggregate rate and every per-type rate. The raw `/api/market/helix/signal-outcomes` route (desk `SignalOutcomeTracker`) shares `summarizeHelixSignalOutcomes`, so the new span fields are available to the desk UI too (it can now label the tracker's window). |
| **Fix** | `HelixOutcomeDistribution` gains `gradedOldestFiredAt`/`gradedNewestFiredAt` — the fired_at span of the GRADED rows (not the fetched set, whose newest rows are today's still-pending fires the rate does not cover), computed purely in `distributionOf` via a `firedAtSpan` helper that keeps the RAW ledger string (no timezone reinterpretation in the pure layer) and skips unparseable timestamps. `helixSignalOutcomesForLargo` projects them to a model-facing `graded_window` (`oldest_session`/`newest_session` in ET via `sessionDateForTimestamp`, raw ISO kept for sorting, unrounded `span_hours`) on the aggregate AND on each `by_signal_type` row — each type carries its own window because split_flow and velocity_spike do not fire on the same cadence. Tool-def instructs the model to quote the rate as "X% over N fires between <oldest_session> and <newest_session>", never as "today" unless `newest_session` is today's `session_date`. |
| **What was deliberately NOT changed** | The span describes the GRADED population (the rate's own denominator), not the fetched set — a pinned test proves a newer PENDING row does not widen it. `as_of` stays the READ time (it is honest as that; it was never the data time). The 50-row fetch limit and `MIN_GRADED_SAMPLE_FOR_WIN_RATE` null-rate discipline are unchanged. |
| **Regression guard** | +6 tests in `helix-signal-outcome-summary.test.ts`: the span bounds the graded rows and a newer pending row is excluded; the raw string is preserved unparsed; the span is null when nothing is graded (never a fabricated instant); an unparseable fired_at is skipped, not poisoned to Invalid Date; each signal type carries its own span. |
| **Gates on Node 20.20.2** | `npx tsc --noEmit` clean · `helix-signal-outcome-summary.test.ts` 17/17 · validated live against production rows (pre-deploy). |
| **Status** | FIXED — this PR. Not yet live-verified end-to-end through the Largo tool (held by the pure-function tests + the live-rows run; the `graded_window` fields must be re-read through `get_helix_signal_outcomes` once deployed). |

## 2026-08-21 — [FINDING, P1 Meridian] Every name that reported this morning was still headlined "Imminent print — stand aside for reaction" — FIXED

> **kind:** `FINDING`

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Symptom** | Measured on production 2026-08-21 at 12:52 ET. All THREE names that reported that morning were still carrying, as the Report tab's primary `<h3>` (`MeridianEarningsReportPanel.tsx:134` renders `report.headline`), the sentence **"Imminent print — stand aside for reaction"** — roughly six hours after their numbers were public: `BEKE` 06:00 ET (`post_print` "Beat · EPS +50% · Rev +3%", verdict bullish), `BJ` 06:45 ET ("Beat · EPS +14.3% · Rev +8.9%", bullish), `BKE` 06:50 ET ("Mixed print vs street", neutral). The advisory read carried the matching line "Print is imminent — gap risk dominates; size down or wait for reaction". |
| **Why it is a correctness fault, not a wording nit** | The headline is a false statement of fact about a scheduled event, and the advice attached to it ("stand aside for reaction") is premised on the event being ahead. A member reading the panel at midday is told to wait for something that already happened, on a name whose reaction is the only thing left to trade. |
| **Root cause** | `const imminent = input.days_until != null && input.days_until <= 1` — a DISTANCE in days, used as if it were a STATE. On the day of a BMO print it stays true for the entire session, including the hours after the company reported. The contradiction is internal and two lines wide: `hasFreshPrint` is derived from the same `post_print` data on the very next line and is used to set the verdict, so `buildMeridianEarningsReport` already knew the numbers were out — it set the verdict BECAUSE they were — and then headlined them as still to come. `buildErPlayRead` has the same `imminent` definition and no print-state field at all. |
| **Fix** | A separate `printed = post_print != null && post_print.lean !== "unknown"` (so an INLINE print counts — a mixed print is still a print, which is what `BKE` requires), applied to the two places that make a forward-looking CLAIM: the headline, which now names what the print did, and the confidence hedge. `buildErPlayRead` gains an optional `printed?: boolean` — optional so every existing caller keeps its behaviour — threaded from `meridian-earnings-intel.ts` off the same `post_print` signal. |
| **Deliberately NOT changed** | `imminent` keeps its original day-distance meaning. The verdict falls through to the pre-print signal stack on `!imminent`, so widening it there would silently re-route an inline print (printed, but not `hasFreshPrint`) out of its neutral verdict and into a score that describes ANTICIPATION — flipping `BKE` bullish off a number that no longer applies. That over-broad variant was written first, caught by a test, and reverted; a test now pins it. |
| **Second effect, called out because it is a behaviour change** | `confidence` was pinned to "low" whenever `imminent`. That hedge exists because an UNKNOWN upcoming print dominates any signal stack; once the numbers are out the uncertainty it guards against is resolved, so holding "low" for the rest of the session understates a read the print itself informed. It is now score-derived post-print — allowed to rise, not forced to. |
| **Regression guard** | 4 tests in `meridian-earnings-report-core.test.ts` (10 in the file), built on the file's own `baseInput` rather than a hand-rolled partial. All three measured names are replayed by lean (beat/beat/inline) and must not be headlined "imminent" — nor fall through to "into earnings", which is equally forward-looking. An actually-upcoming print, and an `unknown` lean, must KEEP the imminent headline so the guard does not swallow the case the sentence exists for. The confidence test is deliberately built on the aligned-bullish fixture so the value can actually rise; a weak fixture would stay "low" either way and pin nothing. |
| **Non-vacuity** | Three mutations, suite re-run on each: headline branching on `imminent` alone (the shipped code) -> the printed-headline test fails; confidence pinned on `imminent` alone -> the confidence test fails; the over-broad `imminent = !printed && ...` -> the printed-headline AND verdict-untouched tests fail. Note the FIRST version of the confidence test was vacuous — it asserted only that the value was one of three valid strings — and was caught by this same mutation pass and rewritten. |
| **Gates on Node 20.20.2** | `npx tsc --noEmit` clean · `npm test` **9420 pass / 0 fail / 1 skipped** · `npm run build` clean · `npx eslint` (4 changed files) clean. |
| **Status** | FIXED — this PR (draft). NOT yet live-verified: on the next session with a BMO print, confirm after the print lands that the Report headline names the reaction rather than "Imminent print", and that the advisory read drops the gap-risk line. |

## 2026-08-21 — [FINDING, P1 Meridian/UW] A dark-pool fetch that never got an answer was served as "No large dark pool prints today" — and cached — FIXED

> **kind:** `FINDING`

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Symptom** | Same event, same session, ~30 minutes apart on production. `earnings:BEKE:2026-08-21` rendered `Dark pool $2.2M · largest first · 9 print(s) | $2.19M` in the live DOM at ~11:33 ET (Positioning) and again at ~11:53 ET (Report). From 12:25 ET the API served `available:false`, zero prints, and **`detail: "No large dark pool prints today"`** — stable across three reads 20s apart, so it was being served consistently rather than flickering. |
| **Why that cannot be true** | Dark-pool prints are executed trades already reported to the tape. The set for a session is monotonically non-decreasing while that session runs, so 9 -> 0 is not something that can be true of the day. One of the two readings is false, and it is the later one. |
| **Root cause** | `fetchUwDarkPool` did `const rows = extractRows(await uwGetSafe(...)); if (!rows.length) return { ...zeros, detail: "No large dark pool prints today" }`. `uwGetSafe` **never throws** — it returns `null` when UW is not configured, when the circuit breaker is open with no stale cache, on a 403, and when its retries are exhausted. `extractRows(null)` is `[]`. So "the upstream did not answer" and "the upstream answered, and there were none" produced the *same object*, and that object carries a positive claim about the whole trading day. |
| **Made durable by the cache** | The fetcher is wrapped in `uwCacheGet(..., UW_CACHE_TTL.darkPoolTicker, ...)`, so a single failed fetch is stored as that false sentence and re-served for the TTL. That is why three consecutive reads agreed — it was one cached negative, not three observations. |
| **The rule it breaks** | Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence; inference must never be presented as fact. This is the same family as the `Number(null) === 0` defects this log keeps recording, one level up: not a missing number coerced to zero, but a missing ANSWER coerced into a finding. |
| **Fix** | One guard, before the collapse: `if (data == null) return null;` — unknown returns null and makes no claim. The sentence moves into an exported `emptyDarkPoolSnapshot()` so it has exactly one home and is reachable only on the path where the upstream actually answered. |
| **Blast radius — all three consumers were already null-safe** | `meridian-earnings-event-load.ts` calls it with `.catch(() => null)` and `shapeMeridianDarkPool(null)` already emits `detail: null`, i.e. no claim — the shaper was correct all along and was simply never given the chance, because the provider manufactured a non-null snapshot with the claim baked in first. `api/market/gex-heatmap`'s `buildDarkPoolLevels` already does `if (!snapshot || !snapshot.prints.length) return null`, so a null snapshot behaves exactly as before. `api/cron/uw-cache-refresh` only warms the cache. The change can only ever make the product report LESS; it cannot introduce a wrong number. `fetchUwDarkPoolRecent` (the market-wide variant behind the Discord cron) is a separate function and is not touched. |
| **Regression guard** | 3 tests in `unusual-whales.test.ts` (18 in the file). `emptyDarkPoolSnapshot()` is pinned to the exact sentence, so it cannot be reworded into something vaguer and quietly reused for the unknown case. A source guard asserts the `data == null` return exists AND sits **before** `extractRows` — after it, null has already collapsed into an empty array and the two cases are indistinguishable again — and that the claim is not rebuilt inline anywhere. A contract test asserts `shapeMeridianDarkPool(null)` yields `detail: null` while a genuine empty answer still carries the sentence through. |
| **Non-vacuity** | Three mutations, suite re-run on each: the shipped code (no guard, claim inline) -> the source-guard test fails; the guard moved AFTER `extractRows` -> the same test fails on ordering; the sentence reworded -> 2 tests fail. |
| **Gates on Node 20.20.2** | `npx tsc --noEmit` clean · `npm test` **9400 pass / 0 fail / 1 skipped** · `npm run build` clean · `npx eslint` (2 changed files) clean. |
| **Status** | FIXED — this PR (draft). NOT yet live-verified: once deployed, a ticker whose UW dark-pool fetch fails must render no claim rather than "No large dark pool prints today". Note the observed BEKE case will not necessarily reproduce on demand — it depends on an upstream failure — so verification is that the CLAIM path is unreachable without an answer, plus the cached-negative behaviour disappearing. |

## 2026-08-21 — [FINDING, P1 Largo/Night Hawk] Four lane tools published fabricated zeros on a failed read — including "the gate blocked nothing" — FIXED

> **kind:** `FINDING`

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Symptom** | Auditing every tool in the lane for the "which empty is this" rule after #2477/#2492/#2495, four more were filling their unavailable branches with numbers they had not measured. `graderAgreementForLargo` returned `total_plays: 0, comparable: 0, agreed: 0, disagreements: []` on both a missing database and a thrown query. `gateBlockedValueForLargo` returned **five** zero totals and `by_gate: []`. `horizonOutcomesForLargo` returned `outcomes: []`. `bangerBoardForLargo` returned `open: [], closed: []` on all three of its failure branches. |
| **The tell** | In `graderAgreementForLargo`'s own return object, `agreement_pct` was correctly `null` while `total_plays`, `comparable` and `agreed` were `0`. **The rate knew it had not been measured; the counts did not.** One object, two standards, and the model has no way to tell that `0` came from a failed connection rather than from an empty window. |
| **The worst instance** | `gateBlockedValueForLargo` returning `blocked_total: 0` on a **failed** read. The publish gate's entire value proposition is the count of bad plays it stopped, so a broken read published the gate as having done nothing at all. |
| **The inverse defect, same two files** | `available: cmp.comparable > 0` and `available: inputs.length > 0` reported a **successful** read of a quiet window as if the tool were unavailable. "The publish gate blocked nothing in 30 days" is a real measurement — and an important one, since a gate that never fires may be miscalibrated — but Largo could never say it, because the payload told the model there was no data. Worse for the grader: `available: false` also discarded `total_plays`, which had genuinely been measured. Both now report `available: true` whenever the read succeeded, with the missing RATE left null and a note saying the emptiness was measured. |
| **Fix — two shapes, on purpose** | A scalar that was not measured is **`null`**: present, and unmistakably not a number. A list that was not measured is **absent**, because an empty array is countable and invites exactly the "0 disagreements" / "0 open positions" claim that is the defect. `GraderAgreementForLargo` and `GateValueForLargo` gained `number \| null` counts and optional list fields; `horizonOutcomesForLargo` and `bangerBoardForLargo` simply stop emitting their lists on failure, each with a note saying not to report zero. |
| **An `outcomes` key that only existed when it was empty** | `horizonOutcomesForLargo`'s SUCCESS path returns `sample`; only its two failure paths returned `outcomes`. So the one time this payload carried an `outcomes` array was when there were none — precisely backwards. |
| **Blast radius** | `evidence-reads.ts` (`get_gate_blocked_value`, `get_grader_agreement`), `product-reads.ts` (`get_horizon_outcomes`, `get_banger_board`) — four of my lane's tools, at the Largo boundary. `GateValueForLargo`/`GraderAgreementForLargo` have no consumers outside these two files, so widening the counts to nullable touches nothing else. No provider, no API route, no UI, no cron, no grading. |
| **Regression guard** | `evidence-reads.test.ts` (+4): a failed grader read reports null counts and no `disagreements` list; a failed gate-value read reports null totals and no `by_gate`; both still state the window they could not measure; and `compareGraderLanes([])` keeps its **real** zeros, because a measured window of no rows genuinely is 0 plays and nulling that would trade one lie for another. The tests mock the db module rather than depending on whether a `DATABASE_URL` happens to resolve — which also cut them from ~20s of connection timeouts to under 1s. |
| **Not a trading-behaviour change** | No gate, rail, sizing, exit rule or grading function is touched — this changes how gate and grader RESULTS are reported, not how anything is gated or graded. No `sim:0dte` before/after is owed. |
| **Gates** | `npm test` **9049 pass / 0 fail / 1 skipped** (Node 20.20.2) · `tsc --noEmit` clean · `eslint` clean. |
| **Status** | FIXED. |

## 2026-08-21 — [FINDING, P2 audit-tooling] The GEX wall verifier still asserted the pre-#2417 unconstrained argmin — a confident FAIL on healthy data on 16 of 26 open-session passes — FIXED

> **kind:** `FINDING`

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Symptom** | `data-validator.mjs` reported `[FAIL] gex walls match their definition` against production during the 09:30 ET open, and the FAIL "self-cleared" on the next run — the classic signature of a timing race. Two operator runs seven minutes apart each produced one FAIL, a different one each time. Read as flakiness, it would have been dismissed; read as a product defect, it would have sent someone hunting a member-visible bug in the served put wall. It was neither. |
| **Root cause** | The wall DEFINITION moved and the audit-side verifier did not follow. #2417 (2026-08-20) then #2521 (2026-08-21 10:38 UTC) made every production wall producer **side-constrained** — a call wall must sit above spot, a put wall below it — via `wallsFromStrikeTotals(strikeTotals, spot)` (`src/lib/providers/gex-cross-validation-core.ts:39`). #2566 aligned the IN-APP verifier (`src/lib/correctness/heatmap-verifier.ts` INV-3). `scripts/audit/lib/gex-wall-invariants.mjs` was missed: last touched by #2178 on 2026-08-14, *before the constraint existed*, it kept computing the **unconstrained global argmin/argmax**. The two rules differ only when the unconstrained extreme sits on the wrong side of spot — i.e. exactly when spot is parked near a heavy strike and ticking across it, which is what the open does. |
| **Why it looked like skew** | The check reads `put_wall` from `/api/market/gex-positioning` and `strike_totals` from `/api/market/gex-heatmap` — two endpoints, two instants — so skew was the natural hypothesis. It is wrong, and the measurement says so three ways. |
| **Evidence (live, SPY, 26 passes every ~90s, 13:48–14:29 UTC across the 2026-08-21 open, market OPEN/RTH)** | **(1)** The same check run **inside a single payload** — the heatmap's own walls against its own `strike_totals` and its own spot, where skew is **zero by construction** — fails on the **same 16/26 passes**. Skew cannot explain a mismatch that exists inside one response. **(2)** The `asof` skew distributions of failing and passing passes are indistinguishable (both p50 0.00s); both groups have a p50 of **0.00s**, and the **largest** skew observed — **60.68s** — was on a **PASSING** pass, while the failing group tops out at 37.58s and has a 0.00s median. **(3)** The verdict is predicted **26/26** by one deterministic condition — *the unconstrained argmin strike is not strictly below spot*. Spot 765.05 → pass, 764.87 → FAIL, 765.14 → pass, 765.01 → pass, then 764.53/764.40/764.53/764.61/764.57 → FAIL. The margin at the flip is **13 cents**, and one pass sat exactly on it (spot 765.00, strike 765 — excluded, because the constraint is strict). |
| **The numbers** | At spot 764.87 the whole book's most-negative strike is **765 (−2.936e9)** — but 765 sits **above** spot, so the side constraint excludes it and production correctly serves **760 (−1.962e9)**, the strongest negative strike *below* spot. The stale verifier expected 765 and called the correct answer a defect. Re-deriving with the constrained rule reproduces the **served** walls on **26/26** captured payloads; replaying the pre-fix library over those same payloads false-FAILs **16/26 (62%)**. |
| **Is the served wall wrong? No.** | The member-visible product is CORRECT and was left unchanged. #2417's own measurement is why: a put wall above spot is support above price, which reads as "we are through support" when the engine means no such thing (AAPL 312.66 with call_wall 310; SPY 763.11 with put_wall 765 — the identical strike pair seen here). The defect is entirely in the checking tool. |
| **Blast radius** | `checkWallInvariants` has exactly two consumers: `scripts/audit/data-validator.mjs` and its own unit test — verified by grep, so no other harness inherited the stale rule. Two of the lib's own test fixtures also encoded the pre-#2417 contract (the 2026-08-14 SPX book asserting `put_wall 8000` above spot, and an NVDA fixture with `call_wall 225` below spot 225.97) and were updated with the reason recorded inline; they were correct when written and are simply describing a definition production no longer ships. |
| **Fix** | `gex-wall-invariants.mjs` now derives walls with the same side constraint as production, matching `wallsFromStrikeTotals` behaviour-for-behaviour including the two load-bearing details a rewrite loses: accumulators start at 0 (so a put wall needs strictly negative gamma — an all-positive book has **no** put wall, not the least-positive strike), and there is **no fallback to the wrong side** (null, because "there is no put wall below spot in this book" is true and inventing one is not). A missing spot now **SKIPS** rather than silently falling back to the old rule — asserting a definition production does not use is how this bug produced confident FAILs. |
| **Fix (validator)** | The primary assertion is now made **entirely inside the heatmap payload** — its walls, its totals, its spot — so it has zero skew by construction and is a real invariant rather than a race. Constraining one endpoint's totals with the *other* endpoint's spot was a second latent instance of the same bug. Cross-endpoint agreement is still checked, **gated on the two payloads' own `asof` stamps**: identical stamps mean one snapshot, so a disagreement there FAILS as structural; differing stamps are reported as INFO with the measured skew. That uses timestamps the payloads already carry instead of inventing a tolerance. Measured over 26 passes: stamps matched exactly on **16/26**, and positioning/heatmap walls agreed **25/26**. The single disagreement (pass #25: positioning spot 765.02 served put 765, heatmap spot 765.00 served put 760 — both individually correct, their spots straddling the strike) carried **different** `asof` values and is therefore reported as INFO, not FAIL. Zero false FAILs from the new cross-endpoint check, and it would still fire on a same-snapshot disagreement. |
| **Fix rationale** | This is not a widened tolerance and not a freshness workaround — both would have been the wrong fix here, and the same-payload result proves it (a same-instant comparison still fails). It is the verifier finally asserting the definition production ships. Deliberately unchanged: the served walls, the `asof` gate's strictness, and the ordering report (now noted as unreachable-by-construction for two non-null side-constrained walls, kept because it still surfaces a null wall). |
| **Regression guard** | The producer-wiring ratchet in `src/lib/providers/wall-side-constraint.test.ts` — which asserts on SOURCE that all five producers pass spot — now also asserts that the **audit-side verifier** applies the constraint, skips without a spot, and that `data-validator` pairs heatmap totals with the heatmap's OWN spot. That ratchet existed and did not cover the audit lib, which is precisely how this shipped. Plus 16 unit tests in `gex-wall-invariants.test.mjs`, including the live 2026-08-21 open payload as a pinned regression and a test that the verdict flips on spot crossing the strike, not on elapsed time. |
| **Gates on Node 20.20.2** | `npx tsc --noEmit` clean · `gex-wall-invariants.test.mjs` 16/16 · `wall-side-constraint.test.ts` 14/14 · full `npm test` (see PR). |
| **Status** | FIXED — this PR (draft). Verified live against production during RTH after the change. |

## 2026-08-21 — [FINDING, P1 tooling] The GEX wall poller claimed `finally` cleanup, had none, and leaked a live admin+premium prod Clerk user on Ctrl-C — FIXED

> **kind:** `FINDING`

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Symptom** | `scripts/audit/gex-wall-snapshot-poll.mjs` header (L39): "Deletes its temp Clerk user in a finally block, same as every other audit harness." The file contained **no `finally` in either form** and no signal handler. Cleanup was three hand-placed `await cleanup()` calls — normal end (L291), one early return (L273), and `main().catch` (L307). |
| **Why the gap matters here specifically** | This harness is documented in its own usage block to run unattended for tens of minutes (`nohup/&/run_in_background`) for "a real multi-tens-of-minutes capture". For a long background poller, **SIGINT/SIGTERM is the normal way it ends**, not an edge case — and that was the one path with no cleanup. The user it mints is admin+premium (L16) on production Clerk and has **no TTL**, so a single Ctrl-C left a privileged live account sitting there until someone found it by hand. |
| **Root cause** | The sentence "same as every other audit harness" was aspirational. The harness it names as its model — `data-validator.mjs` — gets this exactly right: `.finally()` at L757 **and** `process.on("SIGINT"/"SIGTERM")` at L753-754. The poller copied the claim without the mechanism. |
| **Fix** | Cleanup is now literally what the header says: a real `.finally()` on the `main()` chain, plus SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers, mirroring `data-validator.mjs`. `cleanup()` made idempotent (`_cleanedUp`) since finally + signal + early-exit can all reach it in one run. It now also **verifies** the delete with a read-back — a DELETE that 200s and leaves the user alive is the failure mode worth knowing about and is invisible without it. |
| **Regression guard** | 3 tests in `harness-cleanup-contract.test.mjs`. Two are file-specific (SIGINT/SIGTERM registered and reaching `cleanup()`; the delete is verified, not assumed). The third is **fleet-wide**: every harness whose header claims cleanup "in a `finally`" must contain one. That invariant is currently true across all 50 claim-bearing harnesses and would have failed on this file before the fix — verified against the real pre-fix blob from `main`. |
| **The test had the bug it was written to catch** | The fleet-wide scan first extracted the header with `/^\s*\/\*/`, which does not match a file starting with `#!/usr/bin/env node` — so it silently skipped every shebang harness, **including the one it was written for**, and reported a clean pass. 66 of the audit harnesses carry a shebang; the anchor bug hid **20 of the 50** claim-bearing files, a 40% blind spot in a filter whose entire job is not having one. Fixed by stripping the shebang before matching. Recording it because it is the same defect class in the auditing tool itself, caught only by testing the check against a known-bad input instead of trusting a green result. |
| **Status** | FIXED — this PR. Found by the documented-but-unwired ("phantom guards") sweep. |

## 2026-08-21 — [FINDING, P2 BIE/Largo] `ingestBieKnowledge()` silently discarded 26 of 65 docs — including CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and FINDINGS.md itself — and reported `{ stored }` as if the corpus were complete — FIXED

> **kind:** `FINDING`

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Symptom** | Largo's Layer-2 corpus is built by `ingestBieKnowledge()` (`src/lib/bie/knowledge.ts`). Re-derived over the tree at `d30336d`: the walk finds **65** candidate docs, ingests **39**, and discards **26** — 25 past the `slice(0, 40)` file cap and 1 past the 400,000-char size cap. The size-capped file is **`docs/audit/FINDINGS.md` itself** (1,728,097 chars, 4.3× the cap) — the document stored under `kind: "finding"` *is* the findings corpus, and it has not been ingested since it crossed the cap. The 25 dropped by the file cap include **`CLAUDE.md` (64 chunks) and `AGENTS.md` (13 chunks)** — the two documents that define how this platform operates — plus `OUTCOME-GRADING-SPEC.md`, `RUN-LOG.md`, `SYNTHETIC-ORDER-BOOK.md`, every `NIGHTHAWK-*` design doc and every `SWING-*` doc. `ARCHITECTURE.md` line 59 documents L2 as containing "Docs, **FINDINGS**, editions…" — the design of record and the runtime disagreed, and nothing said so. |
| **Root cause (three, all silent)** | **(1) Ordering.** `ROOT_DOCS` were pushed AFTER the directory walk, so `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` landed at positions 64-65 of 65 — mathematically always past a 40-file cap. The two most load-bearing docs in the repo were the only two *guaranteed* never to be ingested. **(2) Silence.** `ingestBieKnowledge` returned `{ stored }` — a count of what went in, with no channel for what did not. `continue` on the size cap and `slice(0, 40)` on the file cap both discard without a trace, so a healthy-looking `bie_knowledge_stored` in the daily `db-cleanup` cron payload is indistinguishable from a truncated one. **(3) Non-determinism.** The walk pushed `readdirSync` order directly. POSIX does not specify readdir order and Node does not sort; it returns sorted on this ext4 sandbox, but production runs an overlayfs image layer — so *which* files fell past the cap was not reproducible across environments. |
| **Exposure window (corrected)** | The brief for this lane dated the FINDINGS.md skip to 2026-07-04 / "seven weeks". Re-derived from history, that is wrong on both counts. Sizing every commit of the file: it first crossed 400,000 bytes on **2026-07-05**, but that lineage was replaced wholesale by the `a05cf324` codebase migration on 2026-07-17 (1,138,031 → 20,545 bytes). In the **current** lineage it crossed at commit **`2c1700f9` on 2026-07-31** (402,987 bytes) and has been over ever since — **21 days**, not seven weeks. Still long enough that nobody noticed, which is the point. |
| **Evidence — cost is NOT the constraint** | Measured with the real `chunkDocument`, extracted verbatim from `embeddings.ts` (2 type annotations stripped; logic byte-identical). Full first ingest of FINDINGS.md: **1,799 chunks · 15 batched Voyage calls · ~464k tokens · ~$0.028 · 17 ms** local chunk+hash. Recurring cost replayed over **31 days of real git history**: day-over-day new-chunk churn is **0.6%–38.4% (median ~2-9%)**, i.e. **$0.0001–$0.0065/day, median ~$0.0004**. Dedup survives edits at the *top* of the file because `chunkDocument` resynchronises — **62.5% of the file's characters sit in paragraphs at or over the 1200-char cap** (single-line table rows), each of which forces its own boundary, so a new entry does not re-chunk the 13k lines below it. A ~3-cent one-off and a sub-cent daily is not a cost ceiling worth discarding the findings corpus for. |
| **Evidence — RETRIEVAL is the constraint (the real root cause)** | `searchKnowledge()` ranks whatever `fetchBieKnowledge()` returns, and that is `SELECT … ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT $1` with `limit = Math.min(opts?.limit ?? 400, 1000)` (`db.ts:7654`). `searchKnowledge` asks for **800**. So retrieval is **a recency window, not the corpus** — anything past the newest 800 chunks is never scored at all, which directly contradicts the function's own comment ("ranks stored chunks by cosine… corpus is thousands of chunks"). Measured composition: today's ingested corpus is **513** doc chunks (289 `doc` + 224 `finding`) and fits. **FINDINGS.md alone is 1,799 chunks — 2.25× the entire window.** Ingesting it whole would fill the window with one file and evict every other doc from Largo's retrieval; the unscoped path (`platform-context.ts:159`, `searchKnowledge(q, 3)`) is the one Largo actually uses. So the briefing's swamping hypothesis is not merely plausible — it is mechanical, and it bites *before* scoring, not as score dilution. |
| **Why the caps were NOT raised** | Every proposed expansion is blocked by the same downstream bound. Raise the size cap → +1,799 chunks, 3.5× the window. Raise the file cap to cover all 65 → 999 file chunks, already over the 800 asked for and near `fetchBieKnowledge`'s hard 1000 once `platform:glossary` (33), `platform:map` (11), `platform:routes` (5), `bie-capabilities` and 60 days of precedents are added. Make the walk recursive → candidates go 65 → 139 (**137 `.md` files exist under `docs/`; only 63 are visible to the three fixed dirs**), turning 26 silent drops into ~99. **Chunking is not the missing piece** — `storeKnowledge` has chunked and batched since the introducing commit `10068d49` (2026-07-02), the same commit that added both caps, so the size skip never protected an unchunked embed call. Expanding ingestion today moves knowledge *into* the store and *out of* reach in the same run. |
| **Fix** | Ordering, determinism and reporting — not tuning. (a) `ROOT_DOCS` now go **first**; the walk is extracted to an exported `ingestCandidateDocs()` and each directory is **sorted**. (b) `ingestBieKnowledge()` returns `{ stored, skipped: SkippedDoc[] }` where each skip carries `source`, `reason` (`file_cap` \| `size_cap` \| `unreadable`) and `detail`, plus a `console.warn` naming every dropped file; the `db-cleanup` cron payload gains `bie_knowledge_skipped` and `bie_knowledge_skipped_docs`. (c) `MAX_INGEST_FILES` / `MAX_DOC_CHARS` / `RETRIEVAL_CANDIDATE_LIMIT` are exported so callers and tests read the same numbers the walk uses. (d) The same rule one layer down: `searchKnowledge` warns when the candidate window is **saturated** (`rows.length >= RETRIEVAL_CANDIDATE_LIMIT`), so the recency-window truncation stops being invisible too. |
| **Blast radius** | `ingestBieKnowledge` has one runtime caller (`api/cron/db-cleanup/route.ts:32`, daily ~3 AM ET) — updated for the new return shape. `searchKnowledge` has three call sites: `platform-context.ts:159` (**unscoped — the Largo path, the one that would have been fully evicted**), `precedent-search.ts:75` (scoped to `kind: "precedent"`, so it has its own window and is unaffected), and `admin/bie-report/route.ts:146` (unscoped, `minSimilarity: 0`). Return-shape change is additive; no consumer of `stored` breaks. Net corpus effect of the ordering fix is an in-cap **trade**: `CLAUDE.md` + `AGENTS.md` (77 chunks) enter, `LIVE-UI-CONNECTION.md` + `MARKET-OPEN-VALIDATION.md` leave — and unlike before, the two that leave are now named in the cron payload. |
| **Deliberately NOT changed** | Both cap *values*, the recursion gap, and `RETRIEVAL_CANDIDATE_LIMIT` (800). Raising the retrieval limit to its 1000 hard cap only moves the cliff and would silently re-tune a number nobody has measured retrieval quality against. The real follow-up is **ranking the corpus instead of its newest slice** — pgvector, or paging every embedded row — and only then revisiting the ingest bounds, most likely via per-entry finding files (which is what the recursion gap actually blocks). |
| **Gates on Node 20.20.2** | `npx tsc --noEmit` clean (0 errors) · `npx tsx --test src/lib/bie/bie.test.ts` **116/116** (4 new) · full `npm test` — see PR. The ordering guard is **non-vacuous**: reverting only `ROOT_DOCS` to last fails it with `AGENTS.md fell outside the first 40 candidates — ROOT_DOCS ordering regressed`, and the test calls the exported `ingestCandidateDocs()` rather than a copy of the walk, so it cannot pass while the source regresses. |
| **Status** | FIXED — this PR (draft). **Not live-verified**: `ingestBieKnowledge` runs behind `dbConfigured()` on the daily cron, and raw Postgres is blocked from this sandbox. The corpus change must be confirmed post-deploy from the `db-cleanup` cron payload (`bie_knowledge_skipped_docs` should name 26 files) and by asking live Largo something only `CLAUDE.md` could answer. |

## 2026-08-21 — [FINDING, P2 Meridian] "100% beat rate over 16 prints" — on a name with 8 prints. A cohort I added, in the wrong unit — FIXED

> **kind:** `FINDING`

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **How it was found** | Largo-mastery stress test: reading the live `intel.report` pillars for NVDA to check whether the desk can answer *"why does it lean that way"*. It can — 9 pillars with lean, weight and evidence. One of them read: `history bullish w=1 score=1 "100% beat rate over 16 prints"`. **NVDA has 8 prints.** |
| **Mine, from earlier today** | #2513 made `combined_beat_rate` **pooled** — `(epsBeats + revBeats) / (epsN + revN)` — which is right, and is what makes a 1-print revenue rate stop outweighing an 8-print EPS rate. But `combined_graded` is then a count of **READINGS**, not prints: 8 prints graded on both measures give 16. I passed that number to `beat_rate_graded`, and both consumers render it as `"over N prints"`. |
| **Why it matters more than a wording slip** | The whole point of #2513 was that a rate without its denominator is not a fact about the company. A rate with the **wrong** denominator is worse — it is a false statement about the sample size, stated confidently, in the one place a reader goes to check the sample size. It also inflates apparent confidence by exactly 2×. |
| **Fix** | `dualBeatRateFromPrints` now also returns `prints_graded` — distinct prints with at least one gradeable measure — and the intel layer passes that to `beat_rate_graded`. `combined_graded` stays, because it is the honest denominator of the pooled rate; its doc comment now says outright that it is readings and must never be rendered as prints. |
| **Either, not both** | `prints_graded` counts a print graded on EITHER measure. A print with revenue but no EPS still happened and still informs the revenue rate; requiring both would undercount the sample in the opposite direction. |
| **Regression guard** | 3 tests in `meridian-benzinga-earnings-core.test.ts`: the live 8-print case reports `combined_graded 16` and `prints_graded 8` with an explicit `notEqual` so conflating them fails; a mixed-grading fixture where 3 of 4 prints contribute something gives `combined_graded 4, prints_graded 3`; and the original 2-print case now asserts both. |
| **Also confirmed by the same probe — not defects** | `intel.report` carries verdict/score/confidence and 9 weighted pillars; `intel.thermal` carries spot, king strike, call/put wall, gamma flip and max pain; `expected_vs_realized` reads `{expected 7.7%, realized -1.77%, ratio 0.23, verdict "under"}` — and **-1.77 is `reaction_pct`, not `session_change_pct`**, so #2488 flows correctly into the implied-vs-realized comparison. I probed `d.report` and `intel.call_wall` first, found nothing, and nearly filed two phantom findings; both live one level down. Recorded so the next reader uses the right paths. |
| **Still genuinely absent** | No explicit conflict/dissent field. The pillar leans make disagreement derivable (NVDA: 5 bullish / 0 bearish / 4 neutral), but a consumer has to compute it. Raised, not fixed here. |
| **Gates on Node 20.20.2** | `npx tsc --noEmit` clean · `npm test` **9300 pass / 0 fail** · `npm run build` clean · `npx eslint` clean. |
| **Status** | FIXED — PR #2563 (draft). |

## 2026-08-21 — [FINDING, P1 Meridian/Largo] A still-moving intraday number was labelled "session_open_to_close" sixteen minutes into the session — FIXED

> **kind:** `FINDING`

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **How it was found** | RTH validation, 09:46 ET, sixteen minutes after the open. Asked what reaction the product reports for prints that landed THIS morning. |
| **Symptom** | Today's BMO prints came back from production as settled measurements: `BEKE reaction_pct -4.74`, `BJ 1.74`, `BKE 2.21` — every one carrying `reaction_measure: "session_open_to_close"` on a session that does not close for another six hours. |
| **Proof it is the partial bar** | BJ (`1.74%`) and BKE (`2.21%`) match Polygon's **in-progress daily bar** for 2026-08-21 to the decimal — a bar whose `c` is simply the last trade so far (BJ 6,232 trades in, BKE 996). And BEKE moved **-4.74 → -4.24 between two reads a minute apart**: the number disproving its own label while being watched. |
| **Nothing marked it** | Scanned the whole event payload for `provisional`, `partial`, `in_progress`, `incomplete`, `settled`, `session_complete`, `is_final`, `live`. **None present.** A six-hour-unfinished figure was shaped exactly like a print from three quarters ago. |
| **Why it is P1 rather than cosmetic** | This is the lane's systemic defect in its purest form — a number arriving without its meaning. `reaction_measure` did not merely omit the caveat, it **asserted a close that had not happened**. A model comparing today's `-4.74` against a settled history of past reactions is comparing a partial to finals and will read a half-formed move as a completed one. |
| **Fix** | Two new `ReactionMeasure` values — `session_open_to_last` and `prior_close_to_last` — plus a derived `reaction_settled: boolean \| null`. The measure changes because the measure is the thing that was false; the boolean exists so a consumer filtering for settled history does not have to know which two of four enum values mean "final". Both carried through to the Largo pack row, since the model is the reader most likely to compare across prints. |
| **`openSessionYmd`** | New pure-apart-from-the-clock helper: the ET date of a session currently open, else null. Bounded 09:30 ≤ t < 16:00 — at exactly 16:00 the bar is final, so the close is strict. Uses `isTradingDayEt`, the **shared** calendar, so a holiday is never treated as an open session; a weekday test would have called Juneteenth open. The clock is a parameter, so the bounds are testable without freezing time. |
| **The value is still reported** | `reaction_pct` keeps its number — it is real, just not final. Only the label changes. A test pins that the same print before and after the close yields the identical arithmetic and differs only in `reaction_measure`/`reaction_settled`. |
| **Fails safe** | `openSessionYmd` defaults to `null` at every call site, so an un-updated caller can only ever report `settled: true` — the pre-existing behaviour — rather than start emitting spurious `false`. Pinned by a test. |
| **Regression guard** | 9 tests in `meridian-open-session.test.ts` — bell bounds at both ends including 16:00 exactly, Juneteenth and a Saturday rejected while an ordinary Tuesday passes, the live BMO case, the same print settled after the close, an AMC print anchored on the open session, **settled history explicitly untouched** (the real risk of this change), `null` rather than `false` when nothing was measured, and the batch threading. Plus 1 in `pre-earnings-history-rows.test.ts`. Non-vacuous: hard-coding `settled = true` fails 3. |
| **Cohort** | The three prints are every earnings row on the `days=2` timeline lane for 2026-08-21, all impacts, after the optionable filter — not a sample. |
| **Gates on Node 20.20.2** | `npx tsc --noEmit` clean · `npm test` **9344 pass / 0 fail** · `npm run build` clean · `npx eslint` clean. |
| **Status** | FIXED — PR #2579 (draft). Found on production during RTH; prod verification owed once it deploys. |

## 2026-08-21 — [FINDING, P2 Largo/Night Hawk] The gate-value tool let Largo print a self-contradictory "3 of 16 (23.1%)" — FIXED

> **kind:** `FINDING`

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Symptom** | Stress-testing live Largo: *"which gate blocked the most winners, and its win rate on the plays it blocked?"* Largo answered **"target_unreachable... 3 of 16 (23.1%)"** and **"stale_quote_basis blocked 7 plays with a 66.7% win rate (4 would have won)"**. Both are internally inconsistent: 3/16 = 18.75%, not 23.1%; 4/7 = 57%, not 66.7%. A member who checks the arithmetic finds it does not add up. |
| **Root cause** | The rate is correct — `would_have_won_rate_pct` is computed server-side over `decisive.length` (wins+losses): 3/13 = 23.1%, 4/6 = 66.7%. But that denominator was **named nowhere in the payload**. The per-gate line shipped `blocked_n`, `graded_n`, `would_have_won` and the rate, so the model paired the correct rate with the most prominent count (`blocked_n`) and printed a number that contradicts itself. Not the model doing bad arithmetic — the model quoting a right rate against a wrong denominator because the right one was invisible. Same lesson as #2480: never make the model choose the denominator. |
| **Fix** | `gateBlockedValue` (pure, `src/features/nighthawk/lib/debrief-aggregate.ts`) now emits two additive fields per gate: `decided_n` (the rate denominator — wins+losses, explicitly NOT `blocked_n` or `graded_n`), and `summary`, a ready-made sentence whose every number already agrees — *"target_unreachable blocked 16; of the 13 that would have decided (win/loss), 3 would have won (23.1%) and 10 would have lost; 3 more would not have filled."* A gate with no decisive counterfactual says *"no win rate to quote"* and renders no percent. The `get_gate_blocked_value` tool description now states the denominator rule outright and tells the model to prefer quoting `summary`. |
| **Blast radius** | Additive fields on `GateBlockedValueLine`; the aggregator and one tool description. The admin dashboard consumer (`AdminBieDashboard.tsx`) reads `by_gate` and is unaffected. No provider, no gate logic, no grading — the numbers are unchanged, only made unambiguous. |
| **Regression guard** | `debrief-aggregate.test.ts` (+1 test, extended another): `decided_n` is wins+losses (not `blocked_n(5)` or `graded_n(4)`); the `summary` sentence's counts all agree so a model cannot print "1 of 5 (33.3%)"; and a gate with no decisive counterfactual quotes no rate and renders no percent. |
| **Not a trading-behaviour change** | No gate threshold, rail, sizing, exit rule or grading function is touched. No `sim:0dte` before/after is owed. |
| **Status** | FIXED. |

## 2026-08-21 — [FINDING, P1 Largo/Night Hawk] `get_nighthawk_horizons` manufactured the empty array it then counted — a 0DTE outage published as `open_count: 0` — FIXED

> **kind:** `FINDING`

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Symptom** | `nighthawkHorizonsForLargo` read the 0DTE lane as `zeroDtePlaysForLargo().catch(() => ({ available: false, plays: [] }))` and counted that array on the very next line. A failed 0DTE read therefore published `zero_dte: { play_count: 0, open_count: 0, sample: [] }` inside an envelope stamped `available: true`. A member asking "what is open right now" during a 0DTE outage was told **nothing is**. |
| **What makes this one worse than a lost error** | The fallback did not merely swallow the failure — it **constructed** the empty array that the next line measured. The zero was not a leftover; it was manufactured on the failure path and then counted as if it had been observed. |
| **The interaction that made it urgent** | #2492 makes `zeroDtePlaysForLargo` **omit `plays` entirely** when the board is unreadable, precisely so that nothing downstream can count zero. This consumer's `Array.isArray(...) ? ... : []` guard converted that honest unknown straight back into `0`. An honest producer is not enough if its consumer launders the answer — the two fixes had to land as a pair or #2492 would have been silently undone one tool over. |
| **Third appearance of one shape** | #2477 (Largo live feed), #2492 (`get_zerodte_plays` itself), and here. Same rule each time: an empty list must say WHICH empty it is, and when the answer is unknown there must be no number present for a model to quote. |
| **Second defect, same function** | `swingHorizonForLargo` passed `fetchOpenSwingPositions().catch(() => [])`, so an unreadable open-positions ledger became "no open swing positions" — again a failure emerging as a measurement, again under `available: true`. The catch has to stay (`serving-lane.ts:160` swallows the throw at its own call site, so letting it propagate only moves the silence), but it now records that it fired and the payload says `degraded: true`, `reason: "open_positions_unreadable"`, with a note that the open/managed counts are not measurements while discovery candidates are unaffected. |
| **Third, smaller** | `swing: swing.available ? swing : { available: false }` discarded the producer's own error string. An unavailable that will not say why is one step better than a fabricated zero and one step worse than an answer; the reason is now carried through. |
| **Fix** | New pure `src/lib/largo/zero-dte-horizon-summary.ts`. `zeroDteHorizonSummary(zerodte)` returns a discriminated result: `{ available: true, play_count, open_count, sample }` only when a real `plays` array was actually read, and otherwise `{ available: false, reason, note }` with **no numeric fields at all**. Three separate inputs map to unknown — the call threw (`null`), the producer said `available: false` (its reason is preserved), or the `plays` key is absent. A **measured** empty session still reports `open_count: 0`, because that is a real answer. |
| **Blast radius** | `nighthawkHorizonsForLargo` and `swingHorizonForLargo` in `product-reads.ts` — `get_nighthawk_horizons` and `get_swing_horizon`, both my lane's tools. No provider, no API route, no UI, no cron, no grading. |
| **Not fixed here, named** | `src/lib/swing/serving-lane.ts:160` swallows the same open-positions failure at its own call site with `.catch(() => [])`. That is the swing lane's file and its root cause to close; my caller detects its own read failure regardless, so this fix does not depend on it. |
| **Regression guard** | `src/lib/largo/zero-dte-horizon-summary.test.ts` (+8, pure): a real read counts what it saw; a MEASURED empty session still reports 0 because that is an answer; a thrown read carries no number to quote; an explicit `available:false` preserves the producer's reason; an absent `plays` key is unknown rather than empty; the two zeros never serialize alike; a malformed row cannot crash the summary or be counted as closed; and the sample stays bounded while the count stays complete. |
| **Not a trading-behaviour change** | No gate, rail, sizing, exit rule or grading function is touched. No `sim:0dte` before/after is owed. |
| **Gates** | `npm test` **9053 pass / 0 fail / 1 skipped** (Node 20.20.2) · `tsc --noEmit` clean · `eslint` clean. |
| **Status** | FIXED. |

## 2026-08-21 — [FINDING, P2 Meridian] The expected-move rail laid out labels against a width 31-43% of the one it drew — labels off the track, prices printed through each other, top row inside the panel head — FIXED

> **kind:** `FINDING`

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Symptom** | Three distinct rendering defects on `.mv-rail` (Meridian earnings Report and Positioning tabs), reproduced identically across two runs of `meridian-interaction-audit.mjs` at 430x932 and confirmed by reading the live boxes out of the DOM (prod, 2026-08-21, BEKE, track 355.22px): (1) `"±2.3% · chain_iv" ∩ "17.00" 50x7px` — the top row of labels rendered **inside `.mv-rail-head`**, over the panel's own title line; (2) `"17.00" ∩ "17.00" 24x12px` with `ay 1380.66 == by 1380.66` — identical y, i.e. two labels drawn at the same tier and the same place, one straight on top of the other, not a near-miss; (3) `put wall 15.00` measured at left `-11.46` against a track starting at `20.39` — **31.85px of the label hanging off the rail**. |
| **Root cause (defect 3, and the root of 1 and 2)** | `MeridianMoveRail` fed `layoutRailLabels` a width estimate of `label.length * 4.9 + 6`. The rail draws `{label} {price}` — so the **price was never counted at all** (on `king 17.00` the uncounted half is the larger half) — and the `4.9` per-char advance was calibrated for what its own comment still called "the 0.46rem mono face" while the stylesheet had since moved to `0.64rem`.
